title: Mohammad Sayeef Alam
text:
Professional Experience
Research Assistant in HTA,March 2026 – Present  PenTAG, University of Exeter Exeter, United Kingdom

Appraise industry-submitted Single Technology Appraisal (STA) decision models to inform NICE reimbursement decisions, evaluating the full continuum from economic literature reviews and evidence synthesis to structural modeling, scenario testing, and sensitivity analyses.
Develop de novo HTA decision models and adapt existing NICE models using R and Excel VBA to support Multiple Technology Appraisal (MTA) projects.
Collaborate within multidisciplinary teams including clinicians, epidemiologists, and statisticians to co-author comprehensive evidence assessment reports that directly advise NICE recommendation committees.
Support appraising and conducting Indirect Treatment Comparisons (ITC), conducting ad-hoc analyses, writing manuscripts, and drafting reports used in policy decision-making.
Execute advanced statistical analyses spanning survival analysis, evidence generation, uncertainty quantification, and Delphi studies to deliver tailored solutions for external consultancy clients.

Associate (Advanced Analytics),July 2021 – February 2022  Parexel Remote, India

Developed dynamic R Shiny applications and interactive dashboards for economic evaluations to support HTA submissions and strategic payer decision-making.
Conducted feasibility assessments, indirect treatment comparisons (ITCs), and complete economic analyses for direct integration into HTA dossiers and regulatory/payer submissions.
Designed dashboards to visualize key clinical endpoints, including survival outcomes, treatment sequences, and demographic summaries tailored for regional stakeholder reporting.
Delivered actionable insights to internal and external stakeholders, iteratively incorporating cross-functional feedback to refine deliverables.




Research Experience
PhD Researcher, April 2022 – March 2026  Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) Trondheim, Norway

Identified 11 celiac disease risk loci by running SAIGE mixed-model GWAS on 17 million variants in ~55,000 participants (~1,100 cases) from the HUNT biobank, correcting for case-control imbalance and relatedness.
Strengthened data quality by applying sample and variant QC to 25 million imputed variants (22 million retained), using KING relatedness estimates and principal components to control population stratification.
Prioritised candidate causal signals by fine-mapping and colocalising the 11 loci, highlighting a non-coding RNA locus near IRX1 suggesting shared immune-mediated genetics with rheumatoid arthritis.
Stratified celiac disease risk by building a Bayesian PRS-CS polygenic risk score (benchmarked against PRSice and LDpred), achieving an AUC of 0.83 in a held-out test set.
Characterised genetic heterogeneity within celiac disease by comparing diagnosed and undiagnosed cases, utilizing LDSC to assess genetic heterogeneity between groups.
Developed and validated predictive machine learning models for undiagnosed celiac disease in HUNT4, comparing elastic net logistic regression, random forest, SVM, neural networks, and Super Learner ensembles (elastic net selected).
Integrated and harmonised real-world data across unique IDs from HUNT surveys, HUNT Biobank, the Norwegian Patient Registry, and clinical journal records to derive ICD-based celiac phenotypes, clinical histories, and causal estimates.
Automated end-to-end GWAS workflows with Snakemake on HUNT Cloud for reproducible analysis, and built an open-source R package migrating legacy health-analytics models into version-controlled, Dockerised pipelines.
Piloted HLA-region imputation with CookHLA and a containerised Michigan Imputation Server to extend HLA coverage in the cohort.
Prototyped a modular R/Shiny tool for Nordic HTA QALY-shortfall analysis across five Nordic countries, reducing ad-hoc requests from external partners.
Mentored two master’s students informally, collaborated with molecular biologists and clinical researchers, and secured competitive funding.

title: Hi there!
text:
I currently work as an health economist at PenTAG, University of Exeter, UK.
I appraise health economic evidence and models submitted as part of single technology assessment (STA) to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) in the UK. Alongside appraisals, I also build de novo / adapt guidance health economic models as part of multiple techonology assessment or consultancy projects.



Picture taken on way to Norwegian course to Dragvoll campus.


Prior to joining PenTAG, I completed my PhD in Genetic Epidemiology from Norwegian University of Science and Technology(NTNU), at the beautiful city of Trondheim 🏔🫎🫐 in Norway 🇳🇴 🥹.
My PhD research focused on developing and applying statistical methods for genetic association studies, poslygenic risk scores with a particular emphasis on autoimmune disease. And prior to my PhD, I worked as an Associate in the Advanced Analytics team at Parexel, providing consulting services to pharmaceutical companies 💊. I worked on various health economic and outcomes research (HEOR) projects, including cost-effectiveness analysis, indirect treatment comparisons, and regressional and survival analysis.

title: Indirect treatment comparisons Part-1
text:
You have a critical decision making problem. You are supposed to deciding the absolute best medication for life threatening condition where 10 different drugs are available. They all have never been tested againasted each other. Testing occured in various combination of drugs, duration and different periods of time.
How do you find the objective truth from all of this?
We usually think medical research is clean and controlled. However, this tells a different story of missing, inconsistent data.
Raw chaotic RCT -> Clean life-saving policy decision
Doing science for writing literature \(\neq\) not equal to doing science for decision making.



Overall baseline natural history model
Relative treatment effects




* Foundational reality of the disease





What happen to a highly specific subgroup of population when given an intervention or placebo.
What does the disease progress naturally? Relapse? Hospitalization? over a given period you need to establish the baseline first |
this is the specific data you extract from RCT to see how the drug alters the baseline tracjectory
Shift cause by the intervention|

For scientific braoad academic reviews you lump everything together and provide the average effect, but for decision making does not help, because of heterogeneity.

title: Indirect treatment comparisons Part-1
text:
Heterogeneity
You can not combine trials of young kids receiving the treatment first time with teenagers who have already failed multiple lines of therapies already. Because there baseline natural history completely different from each other. The average effect hence calculated does not apply to either of the two groups.
Rheumatoid Arthritis - patients are naive to biologic drugs meaning their immune systems have never been exposed to them and we have patients who have tried biologics but either body have developed resistance or failed to respond.
Hence the assumption that these two groups to observe the same treatment effect is absurd.
The mathematical formula might provide you with an average however that estimate is not to be used to explain clinical effect.
Hence the inclusion criteria is to be defined very strictly.

title: Indirect treatment comparisons Part-1
text:
Evidence Synthesis

Heterogeneity
You can not combine trials of young kids receiving the treatment first time with teenagers who have already failed multiple lines of therapies already. Because there baseline natural history completely different from each other. The average effect hence calculated does not apply to either of the two groups.
Rheumatoid Arthritis - patients are naive to biologic drugs meaning their immune systems have never been exposed to them and we have patients who have tried biologics but either body have developed resistance or failed to respond.
Hence the assumption that these two groups to observe the same treatment effect is absurd.
The mathematical formula might provide you with an average however that estimate is not to be used to explain clinical effect.
Hence the inclusion criteria is to be defined very strictly.
Rules for building the evidence network


Synthesis comparator set
To build this we need Decision comparator set - drugs you actually care about - NICE needs to choose between for that specific target population - Drug A, B, C.
Literature search is able to find only Trail AB, there is no Trial BC or Trial AC. Treatment C is ever tested against placebo.
Expand the DCS to SCS: You find a very old Trail AX and another Trial CX, but Drug X is very very old and not used now. Although it would strengthen the overall inference it would have significant risk, namely of effect modifiers.


Effect modifier
Factors that change how the drug works in the real world. Since 1990 when X was tested the diagnostic criteria, SoC changed, maybe severity of illness. Hence the patients that time might be significantly different from today’s patients. Hence the population should be clinically comparable.


Gaming
Researcher deliberately leave out or include specific trials just to nudge the result in the pharma company/academic favour.
To prevent this - once target population and synthesis comparator set, you must include all RCT of that target population, comparing 2 of the treatment in your set.
Philosophy - transperancy over exclusion.
This holds even during non-inferiority studies, i.e., the drug company now has a newer drugs which is cheaper than its older drug, even in this case it cannot exclude the older drug’s trial. NICE strictly forbids such practice even though here we not interested in superiority over non-inferiority.

title: Indirect treatment comparisons Part-1
text:
Genalized Linear models
Now have perfectly map of connected networks, but how can we solve the network.
GLM framework uses Bayesian markov monte carlo simulation.
Fundamental difference between frequentist and bayesian approach
One fixed true treatment effect and estimate from Trial is to guess that number.
Data you actually observed as the fixed reality, and underlying parameter, the effect parameter to have a probability distribution. Data is real and true effect is flexible. You start with prior belief of how the world works then look at the trial data and then update your belief to form a posterior distribution, dynamic way of learning from data.
Less about finding a single number and more about finding the most probable neighborhood where the truth lives based on constantly updating our knowledge.

Fixed effects vs Random effects
Lets say you have five different trials comparing Drug 1 and Drug 2.
Fixed effects model assumes that there is one single universal truth for this drug comparison. It assumes perfect homogeneity, any variation between the trail in London vs trail in NY, is purely due to sampling error.
In medical science perfect homogeneity is rare. Patient in London are different from NY, dosing schedule, etc can varying between the two places.
Random effects model acknowledges this clinical reality. The true treatment effect may vary very slightly from trial to trial. The different trials are not estimating the universal truth, but their own specific truth relative to one another.


Exchangibility
We are assuming that these specific treatment effects from all these different trials come from a common overarching dist visualized a bell curve.
WinBUGS can do this.


Link function
Proability of someone surving ranges from 0-1. Standard linear regression might predict <0 or >1 values. Link function allows the linear function to provide estimate and then inverse link function to being back to 0-1 range.
